clue.text: The French with money put up a bit of their capital

parts.note: LA is the French feminine word for 'the'
tin is old slang for money
to quarter troops is to put them up, giving them lodging

explanation.surface: French investors put their money up to buy a slice of the city of Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' reads as raising money, but it is a verb of lodging. 'Their' points back to the French, so the capital is Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: The Left Bank student district of Paris is a named area, one small section of the French capital city.

clue.text: Zonked out in empty London airport

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it, so these letters go within the shell
an empty word has had its contents removed, leaving just its first and last letters

parts.note: the city name with its middle cleared out

indicators.note: someone zonked is wrecked and befuddled, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A traveller lies asleep, worn out, in a deserted terminal at one of London's airports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Zonked out' reads as one phrase meaning asleep; split it, and 'Zonked' scrambles 'out'. Luton is an airport north of London used by budget airlines.
explanation.definitionFit: Luton is the town in Bedfordshire whose airfield is one of the several international hubs serving greater London.

clue.text: Big cheese and better crackers, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: to top something is to better it
both words are informal for crazy

explanation.surface: It reads like a cheese board order: some fancy cheese and some nicer crackers.
explanation.walkthrough: The food picture hides the slang: 'Big cheese' is an important person, 'better' is a verb, and 'crackers' means mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal idioms for the most important person in an organisation, the boss or leading figure.

clue.text: Settled comfortably in finest lederhosen

indicators.note: being in the following words means sitting inside their run of letters

parts.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone sits snug and comfortable in their very best Bavarian leather shorts.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the word break in 'fiNEST LEDerhosen'. Lederhosen are traditional Bavarian leather shorts.
explanation.definitionFit: To nestle is to settle snugly into a cosy, sheltered position, like a bird in its nest.

clue.text: Showed that lady second-hand clothes

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it up, so one piece is dressed around the other

parts.note: second-hand goods are used ones
the pronoun for a woman already mentioned

explanation.surface: Someone displayed that woman's thrift-shop wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' looks like a noun for the garments on show; it is a verb, putting one piece inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: To show someone to their seat or into a room is to usher them, guiding them there.

clue.text: Run twice round area close to village common? Far from it

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it on both sides

parts.note: the same abbreviation for run again, on the other side

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
A is the standard abbreviation for area
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A jogger does two laps of the green near the village, wondering if it counts as common land.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole closing phrase: the opposite of common.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare is uncommon, seldom found, so it is the very opposite of being ordinary.

clue.text: One might dig up old wine, then go off climbing

parts.note: ex- means former
cava is Spanish sparkling wine

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: food that goes off rots

explanation.surface: An archaeologist unearths ancient wine that has spoiled since it was buried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One might dig up old wine' reads as the definition, but only 'One might dig up' is; 'old wine' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An excavator is a digging machine or person whose job is to remove earth, unearthing things.

clue.text: Encouragement to set off fires

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rallying call to start moving
second meaning: dismisses from a job

explanation.surface: Someone urges an arsonist to start burning things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off fires' reads as one phrase about arson; the split falls after 'set off', and 'fires' means sacks an employee.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss who sacks staff releases them from employment; the same phrase is also a cheer urging a group to begin.

clue.text: Ruddy American abandoning part of his country

indicators.note: to abandon something is to leave it behind, so a letter drops away

parts.note: a state of the USA
A is a standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: A red-faced American emigrates, leaving behind his home state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy' could be a British mild swear word, but here it means red-faced. 'His country' is the USA, so the part is a state.
explanation.definitionFit: A florid complexion is flushed and reddish, the same healthy or high colour as a ruddy face.

clue.text: Legally prevent stimulants and cannabis going around

parts.note: E is ecstasy, so stimulant pills in the plural are Es

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Authorities try to ban the party drugs and weed doing the rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The drugs surface fits the definition perfectly, which hides that the drug words are the letter sources.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, estoppel bars a party from asserting something contrary to what they earlier claimed; the verb means to bar them.

clue.text: Energy-filled, rich pals dancing round

indicators.note: something filled has an extra item put inside it
dancers move about and change places, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Wealthy friends full of energy are dancing in a circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Energy-filled' tells you the extra letter goes in with the dancers before they are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something spherical has the shape of a ball, so it is globe-shaped and circular in every direction.

clue.text: City's fabulous deliveryman with case of Rioja for us

indicators.note: one thing given for another is exchanged for it, so a swap is made

parts.note: the mythical bringer of Christmas presents

indicators.note: a case surrounds its contents, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of the wine
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A city's legendary deliveryman brings a case of Spanish wine for us.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For us' sounds like the wine is a gift to us; instead, the RA replaces the US at the end of the gift-giver's name. Santa Clara is a city in California's Silicon Valley.
explanation.definitionFit: Santa Clara is a Californian municipality in Silicon Valley, and also a city in central Cuba.

clue.text: See 21
Casual labourer not at work, initially

indicators.note: something done initially comes first, so this piece leads the answer

parts.note: someone off is not working that day
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A casual worker takes the day off at the start of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casual labourer' reads as a temp; 'Casual' is the definition, and 'initially' means placed first, not first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An offhand remark or manner is casual, careless and offered without much thought or courtesy.

clue.text: Meat that's given away for a glutton

parts.note: something given away costs nothing
liver is offal eaten as meat

explanation.surface: Offal handed out for nothing is perfect for someone greedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, meat given away is free liver; the answer is that phrase as a compound noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A free-liver indulges freely in food and drink, an excessive eater and drinker much like a greedy gourmand.

clue.text: Wretched Democrat was a turncoat

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for a Democrat
to rat is to desert one's side

explanation.surface: A miserable Democrat defected to the other party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wretched' looks like an adjective describing the Democrat but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dratted is a mild curse word expressing annoyance, like confounded or blasted, which is how wretched is used of things.

clue.text: Fresh paint, kind of white for starters

indicators.note: a fresh version is a new one, so the letters are made over in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
Asti is a white sparkling wine from Piedmont

explanation.surface: A decorator chooses a new coat of paint, a shade of white, to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of white' suggests a paint shade like magnolia; it is a white wine. 'For starters' sounds like 'to begin with' but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasti are Italian appetisers served before the main meal, the plural of antipasto.

clue.text: Hunt down and eat foie gras, say, drinking Bordeaux?

indicators.note: whatever drinks something takes it inside itself

parts.note: foie gras is an example of pâté
Bordeaux is an example of a red wine; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: A gourmet tracks down foie gras and eats it with a glass of claret.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to 'eat', not just 'Hunt down', and 'and eat' does not start the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Predators predate on prey: they seek out animals, catch them and consume them.

clue.text: Work to cut litter, perhaps unwanted ads

indicators.note: something cutting into another piece splits it and sits in the gap

parts.note: a litter is a brood of young animals, e.g. puppies
OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone tries to reduce rubbish, perhaps including junk mail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Litter' reads as rubbish, which suits the unwanted ads, but it means a brood of young animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop-ups are browser windows that open unbidden, usually advertising something the user did not ask to see.

clue.text: Some git potentially displaying character flaw

indicators.note: these letters only potentially form the answer, once they are put in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A git, an obnoxious person in British slang, is likely to show some flaw of character.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is apt: a git is the kind of person prone to this flaw. Git is mild British slang for an unpleasant person.
explanation.definitionFit: Egotism is excessive self-regard and conceit, a fault of personality rather than a skill or habit.

clue.text: When schools work, engaging current caretaker

indicators.note: to engage is to take on or hold, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: schools work in term, as opposed to the holidays
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A school caretaker is taken on during term time when the school is open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caretaker' suggests a school janitor, but here it is an adjective, as in a caretaker government.
explanation.definitionFit: A caretaker manager or government holds office temporarily until a permanent replacement is appointed, just as an interim one does.

clue.text: Someone chanting right behind a fan of Newcastle that's gutted

indicators.note: one thing behind the rest comes after them, so this piece goes last

parts.note: to be into something is to be a fan of it

indicators.note: a gutted word has lost its insides, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: first and last letters of the city
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A Newcastle United supporter, sitting just behind, keeps singing even though gutted by defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' is British slang for bitterly disappointed, fitting a football fan; here it strips the middle of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: To intone is to recite or sing in a level, chanting voice, so an intoner is one who chants.

clue.text: Like a little lamb Mary heartlessly fed cooked leek

indicators.note: food that is fed goes inside, so these letters are placed within
without a heart means without the middle, leaving only the ends

parts.note: first and last letters of the name

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Mary, of the nursery rhyme 'Mary had a little lamb', cruelly feeds her pet cooked leeks.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme is a decoy: Mary is a letter source, and the lamb is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambs are proverbially gentle and docile, so behaving like one means acting submissively and humbly.

clue.text: Park in Jersey

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bring a vehicle to the roadside and stop

explanation.surface: A car park on the island of Jersey.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey looks like the Channel Island, but it is a knitted top; the second sense runs the two words together as one.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver stops at the kerbside to park; and a pullover is a knitted sweater, which the British also call a jersey or jumper.

clue.text: Protection for sportsperson playing home cup tie

indicators.note: playing with things moves them about, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A player needs some safety gear for a cup match at their home ground.
explanation.walkthrough: A cup tie is a British term for a knockout match.
explanation.definitionFit: Boxers and rugby players wear a gumshield guard over their teeth, which protects them from impacts.

clue.text: Chieftain in Middle East stopping revelry, periodically

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so one piece is wedged inside another
something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
ME is the standard abbreviation for the Middle East

explanation.surface: A Middle Eastern ruler puts a stop to partying now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: EMEER is a variant spelling of emir.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or commander, the leader of a tribe or principality in Arab lands.

clue.text: Rent in which side of town?

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it
the sides of a word are its two edges, its first and last letters

parts.note: the two edges of the word
a question of 'which?' asks this or that, offering alternatives joined by or

explanation.surface: A tenant asks in which part of town the rent is cheaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like money paid for housing; it is the past participle of rend, to tear.
explanation.definitionFit: Rent is the old past participle of rend, meaning ripped apart, as in garments rent in grief.

clue.text: Like an automatic response from setter tucking into dessert before noon

indicators.note: coming before means going first, so the next piece follows
to tuck into a place is to slip inside it

parts.note: a meringue dessert with cream and fruit
the setter refers to themselves as I
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: The setter tucks into pudding before midday, a reflex they cannot resist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into dessert' suggests eating, but here the setter sits inside the dessert's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Pavlov's dogs salivated at a bell, so a conditioned reflex response is called Pavlovian.

clue.text: Dabbler following Saint Nick

indicators.note: a thing following comes after, so this piece goes second

parts.note: S is an abbreviation for saint
the teal is a dabbling duck

explanation.surface: An amateur trails after Saint Nicholas, Father Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saint Nick' reads as one name; the split falls between them, and 'Nick' is British slang for steal. A dabbler is a dabbling duck.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to nick something is to pinch or pilfer it, taking it without permission.

clue.text: Heroic sailor one pushed back in the drink

indicators.note: something pushed back is moved further along, so it is lifted out and set in a later spot

parts.note: grand means noble or heroic
a mariner is a seaman
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A brave seaman is shoved overboard into the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The drink' is slang for the sea, which fits the sailor; here it means an alcoholic drink. The I in the sailor moves one place along.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand Marnier is a French orange-flavoured liqueur made with cognac, a branded alcoholic beverage.
